answer:
HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, NLSY79; outcome = college-attendance proxy, NOT verified BA completion):

Among NLSY79 youths, the Black–non-Black difference in the college-experience proxy (ever living in a dorm/fraternity/sorority, 1981–1996) is strongly SES-dependent, and the direction is a widening disadvantage, not a constant advantage: at LOW SES the two groups are statistically indistinguishable (Black 3.4% vs non-Black pooled 3.7%; difference −0.3 pp, 95% CI −1.6 to +0.9), at MIDDLE SES the gap is small and non-significant (5.0% vs 6.5%; −1.5 pp, CI −3.7 to +0.7), but at HIGH SES a large gap opens (8.4% vs 19.3%; −11.0 pp, CI −14.2 to −7.7; non-Black rate ≈ 2.3× the Black rate). In odds terms, the Black-vs-non-Black odds ratio rises from ≈0.87 (near parity) in the low-SES tertile to ≈0.35 in the high-SES tertile (interaction OR black×SES_Low vs High = 2.51, p=0.001; black×SES_Mid = 1.84, p=0.049), and adjusted additive gaps from the logistic model are −0.5, −2.3, and −11.4 pp across Low/Mid/High SES (adjusted for age and sex). Formally: the association between SES and college attendance is much steeper for non-Black youths than for Black youths — a ~5.6× increase from low to high SES among non-Black respondents vs only ~2.5× among Black respondents — so higher family SES converts into college attendance far less strongly for Black students, producing near-parity at the bottom and a substantial gap at the top.

Supporting/transparent splits: the pattern is the same when the comparison group is non-Black non-Hispanic only (2.9%/5.8%/19.0% by tier vs Black 3.4%/5.0%/8.4%; interaction ORs 3.21 Low, 1.99 Mid, both p<0.03) and under all SES-definition sensitivities (parental-education-only tertiles, income-only tertiles, and composite with income-missing indicator). Hispanic-only rates (4.9%/8.2%/21.2%) show that pooling Hispanics into "non-Black" mildly dilutes, but does not create, the high-SES gap. Adding the 1981 ASVAB score attenuates levels slightly but leaves the interaction pattern intact (black×SES_Low OR 2.43, p=0.002) — with the caveat that ASVAB is plausibly post-treatment relative to schooling decisions and is mislabeled in the file (range 165–825, not a Z-score), so it is treated only as a continuous covariate.

Key limitations stated prominently: (1) The dataset contains no BA/degree variable and no post-1979 education measure; the outcome is a college-attendance/experience proxy that misses commuter students, so true BA completion — and any differential undercount by race/SES — cannot be measured here. (2) "Highest grade ≥16" occurs for only n=37 in this file (baseline 1979, ages 14–22) and cannot serve as a completion measure. (3) Observational data: findings describe associations; no causal claims are warranted. (4) NLSY79 oversamples Black and Hispanic youths and no sampling weights are supplied; estimates are unweighted. (5) Complete-case analysis (N=12,532 of 12,686; 154 dropped for lacking all SES components) with missing-indicator sensitivity showing no material change.

payload.hypothesis: The Black-vs-non-Black college-attendance gap in NLSY79 is SES-dependent in a widening pattern: near parity at low SES (3.4% vs 3.7%, −0.3 pp), small non-significant gap at middle SES (5.0% vs 6.5%, −1.5 pp), and a large significant gap at high SES (8.4% vs 19.3%, −11.0 pp; odds ratio ~0.35 vs ~0.87 at low SES; race×SES interaction p≈0.001). SES translates into college attendance far more steeply for non-Black than Black youths, so the Black disadvantage grows with socioeconomic status. This is measured with a dorm/fraternity/sorority residence proxy (1981-1996), not verified BA completion; commuter students are missed, undercounting may be race/SES-differential, data are observational, unweighted, and complete-case.
payload.workflow: 1) Loaded nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61); cleaned invalid grade=95 and identified income topcodes (75,001 in 1979). 2) Outcome: ever-dorm proxy (residence code 3 in any wave 1981-1996). 3) SES composite tertiles from standardized 1979 parental education (max of mom/dad) + 1979 family income (mean of available components). 4) Complete-case primary (N=12,532); race x SES tertile rates with Wilson CIs and rate differences. 5) Logistic regression ever_dorm ~ black x SES_tertile + age + sex (additive + multiplicative interaction); sensitivities: Black vs non-Black-non-Hispanic, parental-ed-only SES, income-only SES, income-missing indicator, ASVAB-adjusted (post-treatment caveat). Artifacts: analysis/nls_ba_analysis.py, analysis/rates_by_race_ses.csv, analysis/model_summary.txt.
